::: {.lede}
This page covers why evaluation is worth doing,
when it has to be decided, and how to choose between the available designs.
:::

::: {.eyebrow}
Two purposes
:::

## Testing and learning only works if you know what to look for

When evaluating projects, we often only assess outputs, because they are the easiest
thing to count. Impact evaluation is what lets you move from measuring outputs to
proving outcomes.

::: {.cards}
::: {.card-e}
#### Outputs
What a programme delivers: grants disbursed, firms enrolled, trainings run.
:::
::: {.card-e}
#### Outcomes
What changes because of it: growth, jobs, innovation, resilience.
:::
:::

Before implementation, map out how a programme's activities are expected to change the problem you are addressing. That shows, in advance, why each step should lead to the next. That causal logic, the how and why behind each step, explains a program's reason for existing. It also tells you what to measure to test whether the
expected change is actually happening.

::: {.chain}
::: {.step}
**Inputs**
:::
::: {.step}
**Activities**
:::
::: {.step}
**Outputs**
:::
::: {.on}
**Outcomes**
:::
:::

This chain is the foundation of a Theory of Change, and having thought it through helps
in designing a strong impact evaluation. There is more on this in
[Theory of Change, Indicators and Data](04-toc.qmd).

## Learning through impact evaluation is a continuous process

Every evaluation raises new questions along with the ones it answers, each round building
on the last. That is how we expand our knowledge of what works, for whom, and under what
conditions, and use it to design better programmes. Exchange within a community of practice
matters, so we can learn from each other, not just from our own results.


::: {.cards}
::: {.card-e}
[Review]{.num}
Review a programme's theory of change, identify risks and learning opportunities.
Review lessons from other settings and countries, adapt them, test them in a new context.
Identify baseline needs of potential beneficiaries in your region.
:::
::: {.card-e}
[Test]{.num}
Test different programme designs and delivery modes to identify what works best.
Assess for whom the programme works best. Address take-up challenges, both over and
undersubscription. Learn about mechanisms, unintended effects, and crowding out.
:::
::: {.card-e}
[Invest]{.num}
Get a quantitative and credible impact estimate that can guide future investments.
Conduct cost-benefit analyses to avoid wasting money and to inform programme decisions.
Scale up based on evidence.
:::
:::


::: {.example .romania}
[The running example: SMART Romania]{.tag}

Throughout this site, we come back to one programme developed as part of the EuroCOMP
Lab to show these ideas in practice: SMART Romania, a digitalisation grant scheme for
micro, small and medium enterprises in North-East Romania, run by the Regional
Development Agency with World Bank support.

```{=html}
<div class="facts">
  <div><div class="k">The programme</div><div class="v">EU-funded grants of EUR 15,000&ndash;100,000 for digital tools, equipment, and services</div></div>
  <div><div class="k">Where</div><div class="v">North-East Romania; run by the regional development agency with World Bank support</div></div>
  <div><div class="k">Who is randomized</div><div class="v">Firms: 1,038 eligible MSMEs, pre-screened via an online application survey</div></div>
  <div><div class="k">The design</div><div class="v">Lottery into a treatment group (grants) and a comparison group: 519 vs. 519, drawn before a notary</div></div>
  <div><div class="k">Outcomes tracked</div><div class="v">Digital adoption (DESI), revenues, profits, employment, productivity</div></div>
  <div><div class="k">Starting point</div><div class="v">Average DESI score of 4.3 out of 12; 67% of firms name lack of finance as their main obstacle</div></div>
</div>
```

### From application to evidence

```{=html}
<div class="flow">
  <div>Application survey</div>
  <div>Lottery</div>
  <div>Digitalization grants</div>
  <div>Follow-up surveys</div>
  <div>Impact evaluation</div>
</div>
```
:::

::: {.eyebrow}
Is it relevant for you
:::

## Think impact evaluation is not relevant for you?

Whether you have sufficient evidence that your programme works, or you are still working
out who it reaches and how to design it, there is a case for evaluation. The starting
question is whether the programme is working as well as it could be.

::: {.compare}
::: {.col-e}
::: {.col-head}
You want to learn who to target and how to design it
:::
::: {.body}
**Too many applicants?** Consider introducing randomisation in the middle ranks.

**Too few applicants?** Consider simplifying access and using an encouragement design.
:::
:::
::: {.col-e}
::: {.col-head}
You know it is effective, but is it efficient?
:::
::: {.body}
**Test how you deliver it.** Compare different ways of delivering the programme to the
same beneficiaries, testing changes that improve efficiency and satisfaction.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.soft-panel}
An impact evaluation is not useful only if you already have enough evidence on returns
for your target group and region, and there is no interest in learning about different
ways of implementing the programme for the same beneficiaries.
:::

::: {.eyebrow}
M&E versus impact evaluation
:::

## Monitoring and evaluation (M&E) vs impact evaluation

::: {.compare}
::: {.col-e}
::: {.col-head}
Monitoring
:::
::: {.body}
Collect data on inputs, outputs, outcomes and participants to

- Improve day-to-day management and decisions
- Make descriptive before and after comparisons
:::
::: {.verdict}
Describes what is happening, but not whether it is because of the intervention.
:::
:::
::: {.col-e}
::: {.col-head}
Impact evaluation
:::
::: {.body}
Collect data on participants and control groups to

- Assess the difference between participating and not
- Establish causality
- Support cost-benefit analysis
:::
::: {.verdict}
Determines impact in a way that can only be attributed to the programme, by
establishing what would have happened without it.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.eyebrow}
Allocating public resources
:::

## What does good allocation of public resources look like?

Not always what you would expect at first glance. Impact evaluation can help improve
allocation.

::: {.compare}
::: {.col-e}
::: {.col-head}
Strategy A: fund the top performers
:::
::: {.body}
Firms that succeed: **80 of 100**

Would have succeeded anyway: 65

Caused by the grant: **15**
:::
::: {.verdict}
Looks stronger: 80 successes.
:::
:::
::: {.col-e}
::: {.col-head}
Strategy B: fund the marginal firm
:::
::: {.body}
Firms that succeed: **55 of 100**

Would have succeeded anyway: 20

Caused by the grant: **35**
:::
::: {.verdict}
Actually causes more impact: 35 caused.
:::
:::
:::

```{=html}
<figure class="fig-e">
<svg viewBox="0 0 660 250" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" role="img" aria-label="Bar chart comparing observed successes with successes caused by the grant for two strategies">
  <line x1="70" y1="200" x2="620" y2="200" stroke="var(--dg-line)" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <text x="60" y="205" text-anchor="end" fill="var(--dg-ink-soft)" font-size="11">0</text>
  <text x="60" y="110" text-anchor="end" fill="var(--dg-ink-soft)" font-size="11">50</text>
  <line x1="70" y1="106" x2="620" y2="106" stroke="var(--dg-rule)" stroke-width="1"/>

  <rect x="140" y="56" width="70" height="144" fill="var(--dg-ink)"/>
  <text x="175" y="48" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="13" font-weight="bold">80</text>
  <rect x="220" y="173" width="70" height="27" fill="var(--dg-accent)"/>
  <text x="255" y="165" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="13" font-weight="bold">15</text>
  <text x="215" y="222" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="12.5" font-weight="bold">Strategy A</text>

  <rect x="390" y="101" width="70" height="99" fill="var(--dg-ink)"/>
  <text x="425" y="93" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="13" font-weight="bold">55</text>
  <rect x="470" y="137" width="70" height="63" fill="var(--dg-accent)"/>
  <text x="505" y="129" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="13" font-weight="bold">35</text>
  <text x="465" y="222" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="12.5" font-weight="bold">Strategy B</text>

  <rect x="140" y="236" width="11" height="11" fill="var(--dg-ink)"/>
  <text x="158" y="246" fill="var(--dg-ink-soft)" font-size="11.5">Observed successes</text>
  <rect x="300" y="236" width="11" height="11" fill="var(--dg-accent)"/>
  <text x="318" y="246" fill="var(--dg-ink-soft)" font-size="11.5">Caused by the grant</text>
</svg>
<figcaption>Raw success counts can be misleading. Programmes should be judged on impact, not on the raw success of hand-picked winners.</figcaption>
</figure>
```

::: {.cards}
::: {.card-e}
#### Deadweight: low additionality
Additionality' is the share of activity that wouldn't have happened without the programme. Top performers would likely have invested anyway, so public funds mostly substitute for money they'd have spent regardless — generating little that's truly additional per euro.
:::
::: {.card-e}
#### Selection bias in measurement
Comparing funded, stronger firms with unfunded, weaker ones credits the programme with
firms' pre-existing quality, not with what the grant did.
:::
::: {.card-e}
#### Where the grant buys most
Support actually changes behaviour for the marginal, constrained firm: the good project
that could not otherwise get funded.
:::
:::


::: {.eyebrow}
The counterfactual
:::

## What exactly is the impact of a programme?

**Definition.** Impact is what happens after a programme is introduced, minus what would
have happened in its absence, the counterfactual.

**The dilemma.** The counterfactual is a "what if" and is unknown to us.

**The solution.** Find a way to construct the counterfactual so impact can be measured.
This can be done in different ways. The methods below show why randomised controlled
trials are considered the gold standard.

```{=html}
<figure class="fig-e">
<svg viewBox="0 0 660 300" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" role="img" aria-label="Line chart showing actual outcomes rising faster than the counterfactual after an intervention, with the gap labelled impact">
  <line x1="80" y1="250" x2="620" y2="250" stroke="var(--dg-line)" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <line x1="80" y1="30" x2="80" y2="250" stroke="var(--dg-line)" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <text x="350" y="278" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink-soft)" font-size="12">Time</text>
  <text x="62" y="140" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink-soft)" font-size="12" transform="rotate(-90 62 140)">Outcome</text>

  <line x1="300" y1="30" x2="300" y2="250" stroke="var(--dg-ink-soft)" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/>
  <text x="300" y="22" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="12" font-weight="bold">Intervention</text>

  <polyline points="100,220 150,205 200,190 250,175 300,160" fill="none" stroke="var(--dg-ink)" stroke-width="2.5"/>
  <polyline points="300,160 370,133 440,106 510,79 580,52" fill="none" stroke="var(--dg-accent)" stroke-width="3.5"/>
  <polyline points="300,160 370,150 440,140 510,130 580,120" fill="none" stroke="var(--dg-ink)" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-dasharray="6 5"/>

  <path d="M598 52 H606 M598 120 H606 M602 52 V120" stroke="var(--dg-ink)" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"/>
  <text x="614" y="90" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="13" font-weight="bold">Impact</text>

  <text x="500" y="40" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="12" font-weight="bold">Actual</text>
  <text x="500" y="145" fill="var(--dg-ink-soft)" font-size="12">Counterfactual</text>
</svg>
<figcaption>Impact is the causal effect of the programme: the gap between what happened and what would have happened.</figcaption>
</figure>
```

::: {.example .romania}
[The impact in the SMART Romania programme]{.tag}

For SMART Romania, the impact is the gap between treatment and comparison firms on
four tracked outcomes: digital adoption, revenue, employment, and productivity.

## Finding the counterfactual

**Strategy.** Find a group of firms that on average look like treated firms would have
looked in the absence of the programme. This group is the comparison group.

::: {.compare}
::: {.col-e}
::: {.col-head}
Randomised controlled trials
:::
::: {.body}
Create the comparison group up front, by randomly assigning who receives the programme.
Randomisation is what guarantees the two groups look the same on average.
:::
:::
::: {.col-e}
::: {.col-head}
Ex-post and quasi-experimental designs
:::
::: {.body}
Look for a suitable comparison group after the programme has already been rolled out,
using natural variation in who received it and who did not.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.caution}
**Selection bias** is the risk that the comparison group does not actually look like the
treatment group on average. If that assumption is wrong, the impact estimate is biased.
:::

::: {.example .romania}
[SMART Romania: what is the counterfactual?]{.tag}

In SMART Romania, the counterfactual is represented by the firms that completed the
online survey and were deemed eligible but that did not receive the grant.

Before any grants were awarded, the selected and non-selected groups looked
statistically the same: identical average DESI score (4.3 of 12), similar firm size, no
significant difference overall. That balance is what makes the non-selected group a
credible stand-in for what the selected firms would have done without the programme.

:::

::: {.eyebrow}
Randomised controlled trials
:::

## What is a randomised controlled trial?

**Intuition.** Randomly assign the programme so one group receives it (the treatment
group) and one does not (the control or comparison group). Because the two groups start
out the same, the control group's outcome shows what would have happened to the treatment
group without the programme.

```{=html}
<figure class="fig-e">
<svg viewBox="0 0 660 300" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" role="img" aria-label="Treatment and control groups start at the same outcome level and diverge after the programme, with the gap labelled impact">
  <line x1="80" y1="250" x2="620" y2="250" stroke="var(--dg-line)" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <line x1="80" y1="30" x2="80" y2="250" stroke="var(--dg-line)" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <text x="350" y="278" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink-soft)" font-size="12">Time</text>
  <text x="62" y="140" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink-soft)" font-size="12" transform="rotate(-90 62 140)">Outcome</text>

  <line x1="300" y1="30" x2="300" y2="250" stroke="var(--dg-ink-soft)" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/>
  <text x="300" y="22" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="12" font-weight="bold">Programme starts</text>
  <text x="190" y="270" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink-soft)" font-size="11.5">Pre</text>
  <text x="450" y="270" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink-soft)" font-size="11.5">Post</text>

  <polyline points="110,200 200,195 300,190" fill="none" stroke="var(--dg-ink)" stroke-width="2.5"/>
  <polyline points="300,190 390,155 480,120 570,85" fill="none" stroke="var(--dg-accent)" stroke-width="3.5"/>
  <polyline points="300,190 390,182 480,174 570,166" fill="none" stroke="var(--dg-ink)" stroke-width="2.5"/>

  <circle cx="110" cy="200" r="5" fill="var(--dg-ink)"/>
  <text x="122" y="192" fill="var(--dg-ink-soft)" font-size="11.5">Same starting point</text>

  <path d="M588 85 H596 M588 166 H596 M592 85 V166" stroke="var(--dg-ink)" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"/>
  <text x="604" y="129" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="13" font-weight="bold">Impact</text>

  <text x="480" y="72" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="12" font-weight="bold">Treatment group</text>
  <text x="480" y="200" fill="var(--dg-ink-soft)" font-size="12">Control group</text>
</svg>
</figure>
```

**Advantage.** RCTs are considered the gold standard of quantitative impact evaluation
because:

- No assumptions about outcome levels or trends between groups are necessary, if
  randomised within groups
- They deliver strong evidence
- They are easy to interpret


::: {.example .romania}
[SMART Romania: randomised controlled trial]{.tag}

Recap: firms first completed an online screening survey. Of the 1 038 found eligible,
519 were then randomly assigned to the treatment group, invited to formally apply for a
grant, and 519 to the comparison group, who received no invitation.

Because the lottery created two comparable groups, the difference between them over time is the impact ofbeing of the program.

```{=html}
<svg viewBox="0 0 680 240" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" role="img" aria-label="1038 eligible firms enter a random draw and are split into a treatment group invited to apply for a grant and a comparison group receiving no invitation">

  <text x="85" y="116" text-anchor="middle" fill="#2B2724" font-size="20" font-weight="bold">1,038</text>
  <text x="85" y="135" text-anchor="middle" fill="#6B6455" font-size="11.5">eligible firms</text>

  <path d="M160 120 H210" stroke="#B9AF95" stroke-width="1.5"/>

  <rect x="210" y="87" width="160" height="66" rx="6" fill="#F2C94C"/>
  <text x="290" y="113" text-anchor="middle" fill="#2B2724" font-size="12.5" font-weight="bold">RANDOM DRAW</text>
  <text x="290" y="132" text-anchor="middle" fill="#2B2724" font-size="11">before a notary</text>

  <path d="M370 120 H400 V50 H430" stroke="#B9AF95" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"/>
  <path d="M370 120 H400 V190 H430" stroke="#B9AF95" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"/>

```
:::

## Randomisation can improve legitimacy and trust in programmes

Randomly selecting beneficiaries among eligible applicants is fair. When more eligible
firms apply than there is budget to fund, a lottery is a transparent way to decide who
gets in. It treats every eligible applicant the same rather than relying on favouritism or
timing.

::: {.soft-panel}
**What "random" means here.** Not randomly sampling a sub-population to study, but
randomly deciding, among firms that already qualify, who receives the programme and who
does not.
:::

```{=html}
<div class="funnel">
  <figure>
    <figcaption>Firms that apply</figcaption>
    <div class="n">24 firms apply</div>
    <div class="dots"><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span></div>
  </figure>
  <figure>

    <div class="dots"><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span class="a"></span><span></span><span></span><span></span><span></span><span></span><span></span><span></span><span></span><span></span><span></span><span></span><span></span><span></span><span></span></div>
  </figure>

  </figure>

```

::: {.example .romania}
[SMART Romania: additional measures to increase trust]{.tag}

SMART Romania's draw was run in front of a notary: the random number seed drawn, the
selection code run, and the resulting balance between groups reviewed, all on the
record. This increased confidence with the firms that selection was fair.
:::

::: {.eyebrow}
When you cannot randomize
:::

## What if you cannot randomise?

An RCT only works if randomization is built in from day one, integrated at design stage
before the programme launches, not added afterward. The comparison group, sample size, and data to collect all depend on those early decisions.
When that is not possible,
quasi-experimental methods are the alternative.

::: {.caution}
Quasi-experimental methods always rely on assumptions, some stronger than others. If those
assumptions do not hold, the impact estimate is biased. Many of these assumptions are not
testable. The credibility of the evaluation depends on the credibility of the assumptions made.
:::

### Pre-post (before and after)

::: {.method}
Method
: Compare programme participants before and after the programme.

Identifying assumption
: In the absence of the programme, participants would have had the same measured outcomes
as before. That means no other factors or events, for example economic shocks, affect the
outcome besides the programme. This is a strong assumption that rarely holds in practice.

::: {.eg}
For example, sales might rise after a grant simply because the whole regional economy is
recovering at the same time, not because of the programme.
:::
:::

```{=html}
<figure class="fig-e">
<svg viewBox="0 0 660 260" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" role="img" aria-label="Pre-post design assumes a flat comparison line, so the whole rise is attributed to the programme">
```

### Simple difference

::: {.method}
Method
: Compare programme participants with non-participants.

Identifying assumption
: There is no difference between participants and non-participants besides programme
participation. The reason for participation must be unrelated to outcomes. Again, this is
unlikely to hold in practice.

::: {.eg}
For example, firms that apply for a grant are often more ambitious or better managed than
those that do not, so they might grow faster regardless of the grant.
:::
:::

```{=html}
<figure class="fig-e">
<svg viewBox="0 0 660 250" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" role="img" aria-label="Participants show higher outcomes than non-participants, but part of the gap is pre-existing firm quality">
  <line x1="90" y1="205" x2="600" y2="205" stroke="var(--dg-line)" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <line x1="90" y1="25" x2="90" y2="205" stroke="var(--dg-line)" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <text x="72" y="115" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink-soft)" font-size="12" transform="rotate(-90 72 115)">Outcome</text>

  <rect x="180" y="60" width="110" height="145" fill="var(--dg-accent)"/>
  <rect x="180" y="130" width="110" height="75" fill="var(--dg-accent-dark)"/>
  <text x="235" y="225" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="12.5" font-weight="bold">Participants</text>

  <rect x="400" y="130" width="110" height="75" fill="var(--dg-ink)"/>
  <text x="455" y="225" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="12.5" font-weight="bold">Non-participants</text>

  <line x1="290" y1="130" x2="400" y2="130" stroke="var(--dg-ink-soft)" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/>

  <path d="M528 60 H536 M528 130 H536 M532 60 V130" stroke="var(--dg-ink)" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"/>
  <text x="544" y="90" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="12" font-weight="bold">Simple</text>
  <text x="544" y="106" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="12" font-weight="bold">difference</text>

  <text x="300" y="172" fill="var(--dg-ink-soft)" font-size="11.5">Unobserved difference,</text>
  <text x="300" y="188" fill="var(--dg-ink-soft)" font-size="11.5">for example firm quality</text>
</svg>
<figcaption>The measured gap mixes the programme effect with differences that were there all along.</figcaption>
</figure>
```

### Difference in differences

::: {.method}
Method
: Find a group with the same trend and compare differences over time.

Identifying assumption
: Any other factors affecting participants over time are the same for non-participants, so
both groups would follow the same trajectory in the absence of treatment. This is the
parallel trends assumption, and it cannot be tested.

::: {.eg}
For example, if grant recipients are concentrated in areas hit harder by a regional
downturn than the comparison firms, their trends could diverge even without the programme.
:::
:::

```{=html}
<figure class="fig-e">
<svg viewBox="0 0 660 260" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" role="img" aria-label="Treatment and comparison groups both rise, but the treatment group rises further; the difference between the two changes is the estimate">
  <line x1="80" y1="215" x2="620" y2="215" stroke="var(--dg-line)" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <line x1="80" y1="25" x2="80" y2="215" stroke="var(--dg-line)" stroke-width="1.5"/>
  <text x="350" y="243" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink-soft)" font-size="12">Time</text>
  <line x1="290" y1="25" x2="290" y2="215" stroke="var(--dg-ink-soft)" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/>
  <text x="290" y="18" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="12" font-weight="bold">Intervention</text>

  <polyline points="120,150 290,130" fill="none" stroke="var(--dg-accent)" stroke-width="3.5"/>
  <polyline points="290,130 560,60" fill="none" stroke="var(--dg-accent)" stroke-width="3.5"/>
  <polyline points="120,190 290,175" fill="none" stroke="var(--dg-ink)" stroke-width="2.5"/>
  <polyline points="290,175 560,145" fill="none" stroke="var(--dg-ink)" stroke-width="2.5"/>

  <path d="M578 60 H586 M578 130 H586 M582 60 V130" stroke="var(--dg-ink)" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"/>
  <text x="594" y="99" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="11.5" font-weight="bold">Diff 1</text>
  <path d="M578 145 H586 M578 175 H586 M582 145 V175" stroke="var(--dg-ink-soft)" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"/>
  <text x="594" y="164" fill="var(--dg-ink-soft)" font-size="11.5">Diff 2</text>

  <text x="380" y="52" fill="var(--dg-ink)" font-size="12" font-weight="bold">Treatment group</text>
  <text x="380" y="178" fill="var(--dg-ink-soft)" font-size="12">Comparison group</text>
</svg>
<figcaption>The estimate is Diff 1 minus Diff 2: how much more the treatment group changed than the comparison group.</figcaption>

```

### Matching

::: {.method}
Method
: Participants are matched with non-participants who share the same observable
characteristics. Matching tries to mimic an RCT. It can be done in different ways: a
participant can be matched with one non-participant, or with a weighted average of all
similar non-participants, where closer matches count more.

Identifying assumption
: There are no differences between participants and matched non-participants in
unobserved characteristics that affect the outcome.

::: {.eg}
For example, two firms matched on size and sector might still differ in the owner's
ambition or management quality, both of which would likely affect outcomes.
:::
:::

### Regression discontinuity design

::: {.method}
Method
: Compare participants who were just eligible with those who were just ineligible. This
does not measure impact for all participants, only for those at the cut-off, which is why
the result is called a local average treatment effect. The advantage is that unobservable
characteristics stop being a concern.

Identifying assumption
: This design assumes that

    - the programme is administered following pre-defined cut-off rules
    - the criteria determining who falls above or below are not manipulated
    - a large number of units sit around the cut-off
    - nothing else changes suddenly at the cut-off

::: {.eg}
For example, if firms know grants are awarded below a certain revenue threshold, some
might understate revenue slightly to stay just below it, so firms just below the cut-off
are no longer comparable to those just above.
:::
:::

```{=html}
<figure class="fig-e">
<svg viewBox="0 0 660 260" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" role="img" aria-label="Outcomes jump discontinuously at the eligibility cutoff">
  <line x1="80" y1="215" x2="620" y2="215" stroke="var(--dg-line)" stroke-width="1.5"/>
```

## Choosing the right evaluation design

```{=html}
<figure class="fig-e">
<svg viewBox="0 0 680 420" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" role="img" aria-label="Decision tree: if you can plan from the outset and have excess demand, use an RCT; otherwise use matching, difference in differences, or regression discontinuity">
```

::: {.eyebrow}
When not to evaluate
:::

## Reasons not to measure impact via policy experimentation

::: {.cards}
::: {.card-e}
[01]{.num}

#### Not the right tool
The question is excellent but is not about impact, for example satisfaction with services
or cost per service. Monitoring and feedback data are easier and do not need a counterfactual.
:::
::: {.card-e}
[02]{.num}

#### Not yet
The theory of change is not clear, or implementation is unlikely to work because the
markets to serve do not exist.
:::
::: {.card-e}
[03]{.num}

#### Statistically not feasible
Too few units or too little money. Large indirect or spillover effects you cannot measure.
Setting too chaotic, for example disaster relief. Treatment assigned at too high a level,
for example national policy.
:::
::: {.card-e}
[04]{.num}

#### Maybe not worth it for learning
The answer is already known from credible existing studies, or there is no generalizable
"why" because the programme is one-off with little scale or replication potential.
:::
:::

::: {.team-note}
**Citation needed**
Adapted from Alex's Bucharest slide deck, which cites the Stanford Social Innovation Review
piece on ten reasons not to measure impact. Confirm how to credit it.
:::

::: {.eyebrow}
Risks
:::

## What can go wrong with a well-designed RCT?

::: {.cards}
::: {.card-e}
[01]{.num}

#### Non-compliance and take-up
Not every firm assigned to a programme ends up participating. Comparing everyone as
originally assigned (the intention-to-treat effect) stays unbiased, since assignment was
random, but it understates the effect on those who actually participated.
:::
::: {.card-e}
[02]{.num}

#### Attrition
Participants may drop out before outcomes can be measured, or stop responding to follow-up
data collection. The risk is that dropout is not random: if struggling firms are the ones
most likely to disappear, the firms you do measure make the programme look better than it is.
:::
::: {.card-e}
[03]{.num}

#### Spillovers and contamination
The comparison group is not always as isolated as it looks. Know-how from a business
training programme can spread by word of mouth to non-participating competitors or
suppliers, so the comparison group partly benefits too, understating the true effect.
:::
:::

::: {.example .romania}
[SMART Romania: the programme did not achieve full take-up]{.tag}

Of the 519 firms selected by lottery, only 393 (75.7%) went on to submit a full funding
proposal, and 333 (64.2%) were eventually contracted.

Because of limited take-up, it is safer to report the intention-to-treat effect,
comparing everyone as originally assigned, even though it understates the effect on the
firms that actually took up the grant.
:::
